name: Majority Complexity
definition: For a nonempty finite binary class $\mathcal H$ on a finite domain, the **Majority Complexity** is the worst-case number of arbitrary equivalence queries used by the following halving algorithm. Start with version space $V=\mathcal H$. If $|V|=1$, output its sole member without another query. Otherwise propose the pointwise majority of $V$, predicting zero at ties. Acceptance terminates; a counterexample $(x,y)$ replaces $V$ by $\{h\in V:h(x)=y\}$. Maximize the query count over targets and valid counterexample choices.
graph_summary: Worst-case equivalence-query count of majority halving, with zero ties and no final confirmation once the target is known.
origin_references: The query-complexity notation $\mathrm{LC}(\mathrm{Halving})$ and its lower-bound analysis appear in \cite{maass1992lower}.

monotonic.proof: Counterexample (with zero tie-breaking): $\mathcal H=\{0000,1000,0100,1100,0010,1010,1110,0001,1001\}$ has majority complexity 2. Its initial majority is $1000$, and each possible counterexample leaves a class of majority complexity at most 1. Removing $1000$ leaves a subfamily whose initial majority is $0000$; a counterexample on the first coordinate leaves $\{1100,1010,1110,1001\}$ of majority complexity 2. Hence the subfamily has majority complexity 3.

p_monotonic.proof: Counterexample (with zero tie-breaking): $\mathcal H=\{10000,01000,00100,11010,01110,11001,10101,11101,11111\}$ has majority complexity 2. Its initial majority is $11100$, and every counterexample branch has complexity at most 1. Projecting away the second coordinate gives $\{0000,1000,0100,1010,0110,1001,1101,1111\}$; its initial majority is $1000$, and a counterexample on its second coordinate leaves a class of majority complexity 2. Thus the projected class has complexity 3.

doubly_monotonic.proof: Doubly monotonicity requires subfamily monotonicity, which is refuted by the recorded majority-complexity counterexample.

strictly_monotonic.proof: Strict monotonicity requires doubly monotonicity, which fails by the recorded subfamily counterexample.

c_monotonic.proof: Counterexample (with zero tie-breaking): $\mathcal H=\{11000,10100,11010,10001,11001,10101,01101,11011,10111\}$ has majority complexity 2. Conditioning the first coordinate to 1 and deleting it gives $\{1000,0100,1010,0001,1001,0101,1011,0111\}$, whose initial majority has a counterexample branch of majority complexity 2 and hence total complexity 3.
